exposed_env.name: Exposed secret files
exposed_env.description: Looks for configuration and secret files, such as .env files, the .git directory or cloud credential files, that anyone on the internet can download from your site.

env_file_exposed.title: Environment file is publicly downloadable: {path}
env_file_exposed.summary: Anyone can download {path} from your site. We counted {secret_count} KEY=VALUE lines in it, which usually means passwords, API keys or database connection strings. We did not store their values.
env_file_exposed.why: A .env file normally holds the keys to everything your app talks to: your database, payment provider, email service and cloud account. Bots scan the internet for this exact file every day. With it, an attacker could read or delete your customer data, send email as you, run up charges on your cloud or AI accounts, or make payments through your account.
env_file_exposed.fix:
1. Assume every value in the file has already been seen. Rotate (change) every key, token and password listed in it first: generate new ones in each provider's dashboard (database, Stripe, AWS, OpenAI, email provider, etc.) and revoke the old ones.
2. Put the new values in your hosting platform's environment variable settings (Vercel, Netlify, Render, Railway, Heroku, etc.) instead of in a file served to the public.
3. Block access to dotfiles on your web server. nginx: add a `location ~ /\.` block containing `deny all;`. Apache: add `RedirectMatch 404 /\..*$` or a `<FilesMatch "^\.">` rule with `Require all denied`.
4. Remove the .env file from your deployed files and from your public or build output folder (for example `public/`, `dist/`, `build/`), and add `.env*` to `.gitignore`.
5. Run the scan again to confirm {path} now returns 403 or 404.

git_repository_exposed.title: Git repository is publicly downloadable: {path}
git_repository_exposed.summary: The Git folder at {path} can be read from your site. With it, someone can usually rebuild your full source code, including its history.
git_repository_exposed.why: Your source code shows an attacker exactly how your app works and where it might be weak. Git history also often contains passwords or API keys that were committed once and later "deleted" but are still stored in older commits. Free tools can download a whole exposed .git folder in minutes.
git_repository_exposed.fix:
1. Check your Git history for secrets (for example with gitleaks or trufflehog). Rotate (change) every key, token or password you find, even old ones, and revoke the old values.
2. Block access to the .git folder on your web server. nginx: add a `location ~ /\.git` block containing `deny all;`. Apache: add `RedirectMatch 404 /\.git`.
3. Remove the .git folder from your deployment. Deploy from a build step or artifact (Vercel, Netlify, Docker image, CI pipeline) instead of copying the whole project folder to the server.
4. Run the scan again to confirm {path} now returns 403 or 404.

cloud_credentials_exposed.title: Cloud credentials file is publicly downloadable: {path}
cloud_credentials_exposed.summary: A cloud access file, such as an AWS credentials file, can be downloaded from {path} on your site.
cloud_credentials_exposed.why: These keys give direct access to your cloud account. An attacker could read or delete your storage buckets and databases, start expensive servers (often for crypto mining) that you will be billed for, or lock you out of your own account. Leaked cloud keys are typically abused within minutes of being found.
cloud_credentials_exposed.fix:
1. Rotate the keys immediately: in your cloud console (for AWS, IAM > Users > Security credentials) create new access keys, then deactivate and delete the exposed ones.
2. Review your cloud account for activity you do not recognize: new users, new servers, unusual billing. AWS CloudTrail and the billing dashboard are good places to start.
3. Block access to dotfiles and dot-folders on your web server. nginx: a `location ~ /\.` block containing `deny all;`. Apache: `RedirectMatch 404 /\..*$`.
4. Remove the credentials file from your deployed files. On cloud servers, prefer IAM roles or your platform's secret manager over key files.
5. Run the scan again to confirm {path} now returns 403 or 404.

security_headers.name: Security headers and cookies
security_headers.description: Checks whether your site sends the HTTP security headers and cookie settings that tell browsers to protect your visitors.

csp_missing.title: No Content-Security-Policy (CSP)
csp_missing.summary: Your site does not send a Content-Security-Policy header, so browsers will run any script that ends up on your pages.
csp_missing.why: CSP is a safety net against cross-site scripting (XSS). If an attacker manages to slip a script into your page, for example through a comment field or a compromised third-party library, CSP can stop the browser from running it. Without it, that script could steal your users' sessions or read what they type.
csp_missing.fix:
1. Start with a policy in report-only mode so nothing breaks: send `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only: default-src 'self'` and check the browser console for what would be blocked.
2. Add the outside domains you really use (analytics, fonts, payment widgets) to the matching directives, such as `script-src`, `style-src`, `img-src` and `connect-src`.
3. When the reports are clean, switch the header name to `Content-Security-Policy`.
4. Where to set it: Next.js: the `headers()` function in `next.config.js`. Express: `helmet()` (its contentSecurityPolicy option). Vercel: `vercel.json` headers. Netlify: a `_headers` file. nginx: `add_header Content-Security-Policy "..." always;`. Cloudflare: a Transform Rule that sets response headers.

hsts_missing.title: No HSTS (Strict-Transport-Security)
hsts_missing.summary: Your site does not send a Strict-Transport-Security header, so browsers are not told to always use HTTPS for it.
hsts_missing.why: Without HSTS, a visitor who types your address or follows an old http:// link starts on an unencrypted connection. On public Wi-Fi, an attacker can intercept that first request and keep the visitor on a fake, unencrypted version of your site, where logins and cookies can be read.
hsts_missing.fix:
1. Make sure your whole site, including subdomains you plan to cover, works over HTTPS.
2. Send the header `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains` on HTTPS responses.
3. Where to set it: nginx: `add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains" always;`. Apache: `Header always set Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains"`. Express: `helmet()` enables it by default. Next.js: `headers()` in `next.config.js`. Cloudflare: SSL/TLS > Edge Certificates > HSTS. Vercel sets it automatically on its domains; check custom setups.
4. If you want, start with a short max-age (for example 86400) and raise it once you are confident.

hsts_weak.title: HSTS duration is too short ({max_age} seconds)
hsts_weak.summary: Your site sends HSTS, but with max-age={max_age} seconds, which is shorter than the recommended minimum of 180 days (15552000 seconds).
hsts_weak.why: HSTS only protects visitors while the browser remembers it. With a short duration, the protection expires quickly, and returning visitors are again open to being downgraded to an unencrypted connection on untrusted networks.
hsts_weak.fix:
1. Raise max-age to at least 15552000 (180 days); one year (31536000) is common: `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains`.
2. Change it wherever the header is set today: your web server config (nginx `add_header`, Apache `Header always set`), `helmet()` options in Express, `headers()` in `next.config.js`, or Cloudflare's HSTS setting.
3. Run the scan again to confirm the new value.

nosniff_missing.title: No X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
nosniff_missing.summary: Your site does not send `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, so browsers may guess the type of a file instead of trusting the type your server declares.
nosniff_missing.why: If users can upload files, an attacker could upload something that looks like an image but that a browser decides to treat as a script or web page. That can lead to cross-site scripting on your domain. This header is a one-line fix that removes the risk.
nosniff_missing.fix:
1. Send the header `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` on all responses.
2. Where to set it: nginx: `add_header X-Content-Type-Options nosniff always;`. Apache: `Header always set X-Content-Type-Options "nosniff"`. Express: `helmet()` adds it by default. Next.js: `headers()` in `next.config.js`. Vercel: `vercel.json` headers. Netlify: `_headers` file.
3. Make sure your server sends the correct Content-Type for each file (for example `text/css` for stylesheets).

clickjacking_unprotected.title: Site can be embedded in other sites (clickjacking)
clickjacking_unprotected.summary: Your site sends neither an X-Frame-Options header nor a CSP frame-ancestors rule, so any other website can load your pages inside an invisible frame.
clickjacking_unprotected.why: In a clickjacking attack, someone loads your page invisibly on top of their own page and tricks your logged-in users into clicking buttons they cannot see, such as "delete account", "change email" or "confirm payment".
clickjacking_unprotected.fix:
1. Decide whether any other site legitimately needs to embed yours. Usually the answer is no.
2. Send `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self'` (or add `frame-ancestors 'self'` to your existing CSP). For older browsers, also send `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN`.
3. Where to set it: nginx: `add_header X-Frame-Options SAMEORIGIN always;`. Apache: `Header always set X-Frame-Options "SAMEORIGIN"`. Express: `helmet()` sets X-Frame-Options by default. Next.js: `headers()` in `next.config.js`. Django: `XFrameOptionsMiddleware` (on by default). Vercel/Netlify: `vercel.json` or `_headers`.

cookie_flags_missing.title: Cookie "{cookie_name}" is missing {missing_flags}
cookie_flags_missing.summary: Your site sets the cookie "{cookie_name}" without these protective flags: {missing_flags}.
cookie_flags_missing.why: Cookies often hold a user's login session. Without Secure, the cookie can be sent over unencrypted HTTP and read on public Wi-Fi. Without HttpOnly, any injected script can read it and take over the account. Without SameSite, other websites can make your users' browsers send it along with forged requests (CSRF).
cookie_flags_missing.fix:
1. Find where "{cookie_name}" is created in your code or framework settings.
2. Add the missing flags. A safe default for session cookies is `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax`. Only leave out HttpOnly if your front-end JavaScript truly needs to read the cookie.
3. Framework settings: Express: `res.cookie(name, value, ...)` with `secure: true`, `httpOnly: true`, `sameSite: 'lax'`, or the same options in express-session. Django: `SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = True`, `CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE = True`, `SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE = 'Lax'`. Flask: `SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = True`, `SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE = 'Lax'`. Laravel: `secure`, `http_only` and `same_site` in `config/session.php`. Rails: `secure: true`, `httponly: true`, `same_site: :lax` on the session store. Next.js: pass the same options when setting cookies.
4. Run the scan again to confirm the flags are present.

tls_cert.name: HTTPS and certificate
tls_cert.description: Checks that your site is served over HTTPS with a valid, trusted, up-to-date certificate and modern TLS versions.

https_unavailable.title: HTTPS is not available
https_unavailable.summary: We could not connect to your site over HTTPS. Visitors can only reach it over unencrypted HTTP.
https_unavailable.why: Without HTTPS, everything sent between your visitors and your site, including passwords, session cookies and personal data, travels in plain text. Anyone on the same network (public Wi-Fi, a compromised router) can read or change it. Browsers also label such sites "Not secure", which costs trust.
https_unavailable.fix:
1. Get a free certificate. Most hosts (Vercel, Netlify, Render, Cloudflare) do this automatically once your domain is connected; check the domain settings in your dashboard.
2. On your own server, use Let's Encrypt with certbot: for example `sudo certbot --nginx -d example.com` or `sudo certbot --apache -d example.com`.
3. Make sure port 443 is open in your firewall and cloud security group.
4. Run the scan again to confirm HTTPS works.

http_not_redirected.title: HTTP does not redirect to HTTPS
http_not_redirected.summary: Your site still answers on plain HTTP without sending visitors to the HTTPS version.
http_not_redirected.why: Visitors who type your address without https://, or follow old links, stay on an unencrypted connection. Their logins and cookies can be read or changed by anyone on the same network.
http_not_redirected.fix:
1. Redirect every HTTP request to HTTPS with a permanent (301) redirect.
2. nginx: in the port 80 server block, add `return 301 https://$host$request_uri;`. Apache: add `Redirect permanent / https://example.com/` in the port 80 virtual host. Cloudflare: turn on SSL/TLS > Edge Certificates > Always Use HTTPS. Vercel and Netlify redirect automatically for connected domains. Django: `SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT = True`. Rails: `config.force_ssl = true`. Laravel/Express: redirect in middleware or at your proxy.
3. After the redirect works, add HSTS so browsers go straight to HTTPS next time.

cert_expired.title: Certificate expired on {expired_on}
cert_expired.summary: Your site's TLS certificate expired on {expired_on}. Browsers now show a full-page security warning to visitors.
cert_expired.why: Most visitors will leave when they see the warning, and those who click through are trained to ignore real warnings. An expired certificate also means your renewal process is broken, so it will happen again.
cert_expired.fix:
1. Renew the certificate now. With Let's Encrypt: `sudo certbot renew`, then reload your web server (`sudo systemctl reload nginx` or `apache2`).
2. On managed hosts (Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare, Render), check the domain settings: renewal usually fails because DNS no longer points to the host. Fix the DNS records and trigger a re-issue.
3. Set up automatic renewal (`sudo certbot renew --dry-run` to test the certbot timer) and an expiry reminder or monitor.
4. Run the scan again to confirm the new certificate is served.

cert_expiring_soon.title: Certificate expires in {days_left} days
cert_expiring_soon.summary: Your site's TLS certificate expires on {expires_on}, which is {days_left} days from now.
cert_expiring_soon.why: When it expires, browsers will show a full-page security warning and most visitors will leave. Certificates from Let's Encrypt normally renew automatically about 30 days before expiry, so seeing this often means automatic renewal is not working.
cert_expiring_soon.fix:
1. Renew now rather than waiting. With Let's Encrypt: `sudo certbot renew`, then reload your web server.
2. Check why automatic renewal did not happen: run `sudo certbot renew --dry-run` and look at the errors. Common causes are a blocked port 80, a changed DNS record or a disabled timer or cron job.
3. On managed hosts (Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare), check that your DNS still points to the host so the platform can renew.
4. Add a calendar reminder or uptime monitor that alerts you before {expires_on}.

cert_hostname_mismatch.title: Certificate does not match {host}
cert_hostname_mismatch.summary: The certificate your server presents is not valid for {host}. Browsers show a security warning when visitors open this address.
cert_hostname_mismatch.why: Browsers block the page because they cannot confirm it is really your site. Visitors either leave or learn to click through warnings, which makes them easier targets for real impersonation attacks.
cert_hostname_mismatch.fix:
1. Get a certificate that covers {host}, for example `sudo certbot --nginx -d {host}` (add every name you use, such as both the bare domain and www, with extra `-d` options).
2. On managed hosts (Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare), add {host} as a domain in the project settings so the platform issues a certificate for it.
3. Check that your web server serves the right certificate for this name (nginx `server_name` and `ssl_certificate` lines, Apache `ServerName`/`ServerAlias` in the 443 virtual host).
4. Run the scan again to confirm.

cert_untrusted.title: Certificate is not trusted
cert_untrusted.summary: Your site's certificate is not trusted by browsers, for example because it is self-signed or the intermediate certificate chain is incomplete.
cert_untrusted.why: Browsers show a full-page warning, so most visitors will leave. Visitors who click through cannot tell your site apart from an attacker's fake, which removes the protection HTTPS is meant to give.
cert_untrusted.fix:
1. Replace a self-signed certificate with one from a trusted authority. Let's Encrypt is free: `sudo certbot --nginx -d example.com` or `--apache`.
2. If you bought a certificate, install the full chain, not only your own certificate. In nginx, `ssl_certificate` should point to the fullchain file (for certbot: `fullchain.pem`). In Apache 2.4.8+, use the full chain file in `SSLCertificateFile`.
3. Reload your web server and run the scan again to confirm.

legacy_tls_supported.title: Outdated protocol {version} is still enabled
legacy_tls_supported.summary: Your server still accepts connections using {version}, an old protocol version that is no longer considered safe.
legacy_tls_supported.why: TLS 1.0 and 1.1 have known weaknesses and are retired by all major browsers. Keeping them enabled lets an attacker on the network try to force a weaker connection, and it can cause compliance checks (for example PCI DSS for payments) to fail.
legacy_tls_supported.fix:
1. Allow only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3.
2. nginx: `ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;`. Apache: `SSLProtocol -all +TLSv1.2 +TLSv1.3`. Cloudflare: SSL/TLS > Edge Certificates > Minimum TLS Version = 1.2. AWS load balancers: choose a TLS 1.2+ security policy.
3. Reload your web server and run the scan again to confirm {version} is no longer accepted.

open_admin.name: Open admin and debug panels
open_admin.description: Looks for admin panels, debug consoles, database tools and status pages that are reachable from the public internet.

debug_console_exposed.title: {product} debug console is publicly reachable
debug_console_exposed.summary: A {product} debug console is open to anyone at {path}. This kind of console lets a visitor run code on your server.
debug_console_exposed.why: This is the same as giving a stranger a command line on your server. An attacker could read all your files and secrets, access your database, install malware or take the server over completely, without needing any password.
debug_console_exposed.fix:
1. Turn off debug mode in production right away. For Flask/Werkzeug: do not use `debug=True` or `FLASK_DEBUG=1`, and run the app with a production server such as gunicorn or uWSGI instead of the built-in development server.
2. Redeploy and confirm {path} no longer responds.
3. Because the console may already have been used, rotate (change) your server's secrets, database passwords and API keys, and check the server for unknown processes or files.
4. Use debug tools only on your own machine, never on a public server.

debug_endpoint_exposed.title: {product} debug endpoint is publicly reachable
debug_endpoint_exposed.summary: A {product} debug or diagnostics page is reachable at {path} without logging in.
debug_endpoint_exposed.why: Debug endpoints show internal details such as environment variables, configuration, recent requests and sometimes session data or passwords. An attacker can use this to collect secrets or hijack sessions, and some endpoints (for example Spring Boot actuator) can even change settings or dump memory.
debug_endpoint_exposed.fix:
1. Disable the tool in production. Spring Boot: expose only `health` via `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health` and protect the rest with Spring Security. Symfony: make sure `APP_ENV=prod` so the profiler is not loaded. Laravel: set `APP_DEBUG=false` and install Telescope/Debugbar only as dev dependencies (or restrict Telescope with its gate). Django: `DEBUG = False`. Rails: run with `RAILS_ENV=production`.
2. If you need the tool in production, put it behind a login and an IP allowlist.
3. Redeploy and confirm {path} returns 403 or 404.
4. If the page showed secrets, rotate (change) them.

db_admin_exposed.title: {product} database admin tool is publicly reachable
db_admin_exposed.summary: The database tool {product} is reachable from the internet at {path}.
db_admin_exposed.why: Database admin tools are a favorite target for automated password-guessing bots. If an attacker gets in, through a weak password or a bug in the tool, they can read, change or delete all of your data. These tools also have a history of security flaws.
db_admin_exposed.fix:
1. Remove {product} from the public server if you do not need it. Connect to your database from your own machine through an SSH tunnel or your cloud provider's console instead.
2. If you must keep it, restrict access by IP. nginx: in the location for {path}, use `allow <your IP>;` followed by `deny all;`. Apache: `Require ip <your IP>`. Or put it behind a VPN or Cloudflare Access.
3. Make sure database users have strong, unique passwords and keep the tool up to date.
4. Run the scan again to confirm {path} is no longer public.

server_status_exposed.title: Server status page is public
server_status_exposed.summary: Your web server's status page is reachable at {path}. It shows live information about requests your server is handling.
server_status_exposed.why: The Apache server-status page can reveal visitor IP addresses, the URLs they are opening (sometimes including tokens in links), internal hostnames and server software details. This helps an attacker map your system and can leak private data.
server_status_exposed.fix:
1. Restrict the page to localhost. Apache: in the `<Location "/server-status">` block, use `Require local` (or `Require ip <your IP>`).
2. If you do not use it, disable it: `sudo a2dismod status` on Debian/Ubuntu, then reload Apache.
3. For nginx `stub_status`, add `allow 127.0.0.1;` and `deny all;` in that location.
4. Run the scan again to confirm {path} returns 403 or 404.

admin_login_exposed.title: Admin login page is publicly reachable
admin_login_exposed.summary: We found an admin login page at {path}. This is common and not a problem on its own, but it is worth limiting.
admin_login_exposed.why: Public login pages are constantly tried by bots that guess common passwords. If an admin account has a weak or reused password and there are no limits on attempts, an attacker may eventually get in.
admin_login_exposed.fix:
1. Use strong, unique passwords for every admin account and turn on two-factor authentication (2FA).
2. Limit login attempts: for example a rate-limit plugin (WordPress), `express-rate-limit` (Express), django-axes (Django), or Cloudflare rate limiting rules.
3. If only your team uses this page, restrict it by IP or put it behind Cloudflare Access or a VPN.
4. Optionally move the admin area to a less obvious path, but treat this only as a small extra, not as protection.

default_creds.name: Unfinished setup and default passwords
default_creds.description: Looks for installers and setup wizards left reachable, and for products that are known to ship with default passwords. It never tries to log in.

installer_exposed.title: {product} installer is still reachable
installer_exposed.summary: The {product} installer is reachable at {path}. If setup was never finished, anyone could complete it.
installer_exposed.why: Whoever completes the installer chooses the admin account. An attacker could finish setup themselves, become the administrator of your site and, in many cases, run their own code on your server. Bots look for unfinished installers within hours of a new site going live.
installer_exposed.fix:
1. Open {path} yourself. If the installer is still offering to set things up, finish the installation now with a strong admin password.
2. Delete or block the installer files: Joomla: remove the `installation` folder. Drupal: block `install.php` at the web server. WordPress: once installed, `wp-admin/install.php` should only say it is already installed; you can also block it in nginx or Apache.
3. If the site was already set up by someone you do not know, take it offline, reinstall from a clean copy, and rotate (change) your database and hosting passwords.
4. Run the scan again to confirm {path} is no longer reachable.

setup_wizard_exposed.title: {product} setup wizard is still open
setup_wizard_exposed.summary: The {product} first-time setup screen is reachable at {path}, which suggests setup was not completed.
setup_wizard_exposed.why: The first person to finish the setup wizard becomes the administrator. For tools like Jenkins, that means full control over your build server, your source code and the secrets it uses to deploy, plus the ability to run commands on the server.
setup_wizard_exposed.fix:
1. Complete the setup yourself right away, and create an admin account with a strong, unique password. For Jenkins, use the unlock key from the server (`/var/lib/jenkins/secrets/initialAdminPassword`).
2. Restrict access to {product} by IP, VPN or Cloudflare Access; build and admin tools rarely need to be public.
3. If you find admin accounts or jobs you did not create, assume the tool was taken over: rebuild it and rotate (change) every secret it stored.
4. Run the scan again to confirm {path} no longer shows the setup screen.

default_login_product.title: {product} login is public; make sure the default password is changed
default_login_product.summary: We found a {product} login at {path}. This product is known to ship with default usernames and passwords. We did not try to log in.
default_login_product.why: Default passwords for products like {product} are published in manuals and are the first thing bots try. If yours was never changed, an attacker can log in as an administrator and, for tools like Tomcat Manager, deploy their own code to your server.
default_login_product.fix:
1. Log in and make sure the default admin password (for example admin/admin for Grafana, or users in Tomcat's `tomcat-users.xml`) has been replaced with a strong, unique one. Remove unused default accounts.
2. Restrict access to {path} by IP, VPN or Cloudflare Access if the public does not need it.
3. Turn on two-factor authentication or single sign-on if {product} supports it, and keep it updated.
4. Run the scan again to confirm {path} is no longer public, or keep it public only if you are sure the defaults are gone.

info_leak.name: Information leaks
info_leak.description: Looks for software versions, error details, debug mode and file listings that your site reveals to visitors.

server_version_disclosed.title: Server version is visible: {value}
server_version_disclosed.summary: Your server's {header} header reveals its software and version: "{value}".
server_version_disclosed.why: This is a small risk on its own. It does, however, let attackers instantly look up known vulnerabilities (CVEs) for that exact version and target your server with matching attacks. Hiding it makes automated targeting harder.
server_version_disclosed.fix:
1. Keep the server software updated; this matters more than hiding the version.
2. Hide the version. nginx: `server_tokens off;` in the http block. Apache: `ServerTokens Prod` and `ServerSignature Off`. IIS: remove the Server header with URL Rewrite or `removeServerHeader` in request filtering.
3. Reload the server and run the scan again to confirm {header} no longer shows a version.

framework_version_disclosed.title: Framework version is visible: {value}
framework_version_disclosed.summary: Your site's {header} header reveals the technology behind it: "{value}".
framework_version_disclosed.why: This tells attackers which framework and version you run, so they can look up known vulnerabilities (CVEs) for it and pick matching attacks. It gives nothing useful to your visitors.
framework_version_disclosed.fix:
1. Keep the framework updated; that matters most.
2. Remove the header. Express: `app.disable('x-powered-by')` or use `helmet()`. Next.js: `poweredByHeader: false` in `next.config.js`. PHP: `expose_php = Off` in php.ini. ASP.NET: `<httpRuntime enableVersionHeader="false" />` in web.config and remove X-Powered-By under customHeaders.
3. You can also strip it at your proxy: nginx `proxy_hide_header X-Powered-By;` or `fastcgi_hide_header X-Powered-By;`.
4. Run the scan again to confirm {header} is gone.

stack_trace_exposed.title: Error page shows technical details
stack_trace_exposed.summary: When an error happens at {path}, your site shows a stack trace: internal code paths, file names and sometimes settings.
stack_trace_exposed.why: Stack traces show attackers how your code is built, which libraries and versions you use, and sometimes database queries or secrets. This makes it much easier to find and exploit a weakness.
stack_trace_exposed.fix:
1. Turn off detailed errors in production (see your framework: Django `DEBUG = False`, Laravel `APP_DEBUG=false`, Rails `RAILS_ENV=production`, Express `NODE_ENV=production` with your own error handler, ASP.NET `customErrors` on).
2. Show a simple, friendly error page to visitors instead.
3. Send the full error details to your logs or an error tracker (for example Sentry) where only your team can see them.
4. Run the scan again to confirm {path} no longer shows a stack trace.

debug_mode_enabled.title: {framework} is running in debug mode
debug_mode_enabled.summary: Your site appears to be running {framework} with debug mode turned on in production.
debug_mode_enabled.why: Debug mode shows detailed error pages with source code, settings and often environment variables or secret keys. Some debug tools, such as older Laravel Ignition versions, have even allowed attackers to run code on the server.
debug_mode_enabled.fix:
1. Turn off debug mode. Django: `DEBUG = False` (and set `ALLOWED_HOSTS`). Laravel: `APP_DEBUG=false` and `APP_ENV=production` in your environment, then `php artisan config:cache`. Rails: run with `RAILS_ENV=production` so `consider_all_requests_local` is false. Flask: do not set `FLASK_DEBUG` or `debug=True`.
2. Redeploy and check that error pages no longer show code or settings.
3. If the debug pages showed any secret keys or passwords, rotate (change) them.
4. Run the scan again to confirm {framework} debug mode is off.

directory_listing_enabled.title: Folder contents are listed publicly
directory_listing_enabled.summary: Opening {path} shows a list of all the files in that folder.
directory_listing_enabled.why: A file listing lets anyone browse files you never meant to link to, such as backups, old exports, configuration files or uploaded documents. Attackers use this to find data and weak spots quickly.
directory_listing_enabled.fix:
1. Turn off directory listing. nginx: make sure `autoindex` is off (it is off by default; remove any `autoindex on;`). Apache: `Options -Indexes` in your config or `.htaccess`. IIS: disable Directory Browsing.
2. Look through the files that were listed at {path} and remove anything that should not be public, such as backups and exports. If any contained passwords or keys, rotate (change) them.
3. Run the scan again to confirm {path} no longer lists files.

tls_config.name: TLS configuration
tls_config.description: Checks how well HTTPS is set up beyond the certificate: which encryption methods your server accepts, whether recorded traffic stays private if your key ever leaks, the certificate chain you send, and your key strength.

weak_cipher_insecure.title: Your server accepts broken encryption ({suite})
weak_cipher_insecure.summary: Your server still agrees to use {suite}, an encryption method that gives little or no protection.
weak_cipher_insecure.why: Some old methods encrypt nothing at all (NULL), do not check who is on the other end (anonymous), or are broken (RC4, DES, export grade). If a visitor's connection ends up using one of them, someone on the same network can read or change everything they send, including passwords and session cookies. Attackers can try to push a connection onto these methods.
weak_cipher_insecure.fix:
1. Allow only modern cipher suites. On nginx: `ssl_ciphers ECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256:ECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256:ECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384:ECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384:ECDHE-ECDSA-CHACHA20-POLY1305:ECDHE-RSA-CHACHA20-POLY1305;` On Apache: the same list in `SSLCipherSuite`.
2. Remove anything with NULL, aNULL, EXPORT, DES, RC4 or MD5 from your cipher settings, including in your load balancer or CDN.
3. Mozilla's SSL Configuration Generator (ssl-config.mozilla.org, "Intermediate") gives a ready-made config for most servers.
4. Reload the server and run the scan again.

weak_cipher_3des.title: Your server still accepts 3DES ({suite})
weak_cipher_3des.summary: Your server agrees to use {suite}, an old encryption method that is no longer considered safe.
weak_cipher_3des.why: 3DES works on small blocks of data. After a very large amount of traffic on one connection, an attacker who can watch and influence that traffic can recover pieces of it (the "Sweet32" attack). It is hard to pull off, so this is a low risk, but no modern browser needs 3DES and it should be switched off.
weak_cipher_3des.fix:
1. Remove 3DES (DES-CBC3, 3DES_EDE) from your cipher list. On nginx, use the modern list from ssl-config.mozilla.org ("Intermediate").
2. In Go-based servers and proxies (for example Traefik), remove every cipher suite name that contains `3DES` from the TLS options.
3. Reload and run the scan again.

no_forward_secrecy.title: Recorded traffic is not protected if your key leaks
no_forward_secrecy.summary: Your server only uses key exchanges without forward secrecy (it chose {suite}).
no_forward_secrecy.why: With forward secrecy, every connection gets its own temporary key. Without it, anyone who records your visitors' encrypted traffic today can decrypt all of it later if your server's private key is ever stolen or leaked. Every modern browser supports forward secrecy, so there is no reason to go without it.
no_forward_secrecy.fix:
1. Enable ECDHE cipher suites and put them first. On nginx: use the "Intermediate" config from ssl-config.mozilla.org.
2. Better still, enable TLS 1.3 (`ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;`), which always uses forward secrecy.
3. Reload and run the scan again.

chain_incomplete.title: Your certificate chain is incomplete
chain_incomplete.summary: Your server sends its certificate but not the intermediate certificate that connects it to a trusted authority ({issuer}).
chain_incomplete.why: Some browsers fetch the missing piece themselves, so the site may look fine to you. But many phones, apps, payment providers' webhooks and command-line tools do not: for them, your site shows a security error or the connection fails.
chain_incomplete.fix:
1. Install the full chain, not just your own certificate. With Let's Encrypt/certbot, point your server at `fullchain.pem`, not `cert.pem` (nginx: `ssl_certificate /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/fullchain.pem;`).
2. With a certificate you bought, append the intermediate certificate(s) from your provider to your certificate file, your certificate first.
3. Reload the server and run the scan again.

cert_weak_key.title: Your certificate key is too weak ({key_type} {bits}-bit)
cert_weak_key.summary: Your certificate uses a {bits}-bit {key_type} key, below today's minimum (RSA 2048-bit, EC 256-bit).
cert_weak_key.why: Short keys can be broken with enough computing power. Anyone who breaks your key can impersonate your site or, without forward secrecy, decrypt recorded traffic. Public certificate authorities have not issued such keys for years, and many clients refuse them.
cert_weak_key.fix:
1. Create a new key of at least RSA 2048-bit or EC P-256 (for example `openssl ecparam -genkey -name prime256v1`, or let certbot create it).
2. Get a new certificate for that key and install it with the full chain.
3. Revoke the old certificate if it was publicly issued, then run the scan again.

tls13_unsupported.title: TLS 1.3 is not enabled
tls13_unsupported.summary: Your server does not offer TLS 1.3, the newest and fastest version of HTTPS.
tls13_unsupported.why: This is not a vulnerability. TLS 1.3 is simpler and safer by design (it always uses forward secrecy and drops old, weak options) and makes connections faster. Supporting it is current best practice.
tls13_unsupported.fix:
1. On nginx 1.13+ with OpenSSL 1.1.1+: `ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;`
2. On Apache 2.4.37+: `SSLProtocol -all +TLSv1.2 +TLSv1.3`
3. Most hosting platforms and CDNs have it on by default; check your TLS settings there.
4. Reload and run the scan again.

http_hardening.name: Browser policies (CORS, CSP quality, framing, referrer)
http_hardening.description: Checks whether the policies that tell browsers how to treat your site actually protect it: who may read your pages with your visitors' logins, whether your Content-Security-Policy really blocks injected scripts, and how links and framing are handled.

cors_any_origin_with_credentials.title: Any website can read your pages as your logged-in visitors
cors_any_origin_with_credentials.summary: Your site answers any origin (we tested {origin}) with Access-Control-Allow-Origin set to that origin and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.
cors_any_origin_with_credentials.why: This tells browsers that every other website may read your responses using your visitor's cookies. If a logged-in user opens a malicious page, that page can load account data, API keys or anything else your site shows them, and send it to the attacker. It is one of the most damaging misconfigurations an API can have.
cors_any_origin_with_credentials.fix:
1. Never copy the request's Origin header into Access-Control-Allow-Origin. Keep an explicit list of the origins that need access (for example your own front-end at https://app.example.com) and only echo an origin that is on that list.
2. Send Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true only for those listed origins, and only if they really need cookies.
3. In frameworks: Express `cors({ origin: ['https://app.example.com'], credentials: true })`, Django `CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS`, Rails `rack-cors` with explicit origins. Avoid "allow all origins" options together with credentials.
4. Deploy and run the scan again.

cors_null_origin_with_credentials.title: Your site trusts the "null" origin with logins
cors_null_origin_with_credentials.summary: Your site answers Origin: null with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: null and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.
cors_null_origin_with_credentials.why: Browsers send Origin: null from sandboxed iframes, local files and some redirects, and any attacker can create such a page. Trusting "null" lets those pages read your responses with your visitor's cookies, for example their account data.
cors_null_origin_with_credentials.fix:
1. Remove "null" from the origins your CORS setup accepts. It is often added by mistake while testing local files.
2. Allow only an explicit list of real origins (https://app.example.com), and send credentials only for them.
3. Deploy and run the scan again.

csp_ineffective.title: Your Content-Security-Policy does not stop injected scripts
csp_ineffective.summary: Your site has a Content-Security-Policy, but it still lets injected scripts run: {reasons}.
csp_ineffective.why: The main job of a CSP is to stop scripts an attacker manages to inject (cross-site scripting). 'unsafe-inline' without a nonce or hash lets any inline script run, and sources like https: or * let scripts load from any website. With these, the policy looks present but gives little protection.
csp_ineffective.fix:
1. Remove 'unsafe-inline' from script-src. Move inline scripts into files, or give each one a nonce (a random value per page load, `script-src 'nonce-RANDOM'`); most frameworks can add nonces for you (Next.js middleware, Helmet for Express, django-csp).
2. Replace broad sources like https: or * with the exact domains you load scripts from, or use a nonce with 'strict-dynamic'.
3. Roll out safely: send the new policy as Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only first, fix what it reports, then switch to enforcing.
4. Run the scan again.

xfo_ineffective.title: Your frame protection header is ignored by browsers
xfo_ineffective.summary: X-Frame-Options is set to "{value}", which browsers do not support, and there is no CSP frame-ancestors rule.
xfo_ineffective.why: Modern browsers ignore X-Frame-Options values other than DENY and SAMEORIGIN (ALLOW-FROM was dropped years ago). Your pages can therefore be loaded invisibly inside another site, where visitors can be tricked into clicking buttons on your site (clickjacking).
xfo_ineffective.fix:
1. If no other site should frame your pages: set `X-Frame-Options: DENY` and add `frame-ancestors 'none'` to your Content-Security-Policy.
2. If one partner site must frame you: use `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors https://partner.example` (that is what replaced ALLOW-FROM) and drop the invalid X-Frame-Options value.
3. Deploy and run the scan again.

referrer_policy_unsafe_url.title: Full page addresses are sent to other websites
referrer_policy_unsafe_url.summary: Your site sets Referrer-Policy: unsafe-url, so browsers send the full address of your pages to every site they link to or load from.
referrer_policy_unsafe_url.why: Page addresses often contain private details: password-reset tokens, invoice or document IDs, search terms, e-mail addresses. With unsafe-url these are sent to third-party sites, including over plain HTTP. Browsers' default policy is much safer.
referrer_policy_unsafe_url.fix:
1. Use `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin` (the browser default) or `no-referrer` if you do not need it at all.
2. Remove the header value unsafe-url wherever it is set (server config, framework security settings, CDN rules).
3. Deploy and run the scan again.

dns_email.name: E-mail spoofing protection and DNS
dns_email.description: Checks whether others can send e-mail that looks like it comes from your domain (SPF, DMARC), and whether your nameservers give away more than they should (open resolver, zone transfer).

spf_allow_all.title: Your SPF record lets anyone send e-mail as {domain}
spf_allow_all.summary: The SPF record of {domain} ends in "+all" (or a bare "all"), which authorises every server in the world to send mail for your domain.
spf_allow_all.why: SPF tells receiving mail servers which servers may send e-mail for your domain. "+all" says "all of them", so fake e-mails pretending to be from you pass the check. They even satisfy DMARC through SPF, which makes phishing in your name, fake invoices or password-reset scams look legitimate.
spf_allow_all.fix:
1. List only the services that really send your mail, and end the record with ~all or -all. For example `v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com include:sendgrid.net -all`.
2. Your e-mail provider's help pages give the exact include for Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, SendGrid, Mailgun, Postmark and others.
3. Change the TXT record at your DNS provider and run the scan again (DNS changes can take a few minutes to an hour).

spf_invalid.title: Your SPF record is broken ({reason})
spf_invalid.summary: Receiving mail servers cannot evaluate the SPF record of {domain} ({reason}), so it protects nothing.
spf_invalid.why: When an SPF record is invalid, for example two separate SPF records, more than 10 DNS lookups through nested includes, a typo, or an include pointing to a domain without SPF, mail servers treat it as a permanent error. Your legitimate mail can land in spam, and spoofed mail is not blocked.
spf_invalid.fix:
1. Keep exactly ONE TXT record that starts with v=spf1; merge any others into it.
2. If there are too many lookups, remove includes for services you no longer use, or replace includes with the ip4:/ip6: ranges your provider publishes.
3. Check the record with a free SPF validator, fix the reported problem, then run the scan again.

spf_missing.title: No SPF record for {domain}
spf_missing.summary: {domain} receives e-mail (it has MX records) but has no SPF record saying which servers may send mail for it.
spf_missing.why: Without SPF, receiving mail servers have no way to tell your real e-mails from fakes, so attackers can more easily send phishing that appears to come from your domain. Many providers also put unauthenticated mail into spam.
spf_missing.fix:
1. Add a TXT record on {domain} listing the services that send your mail, for example `v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com -all` for Google Workspace (your provider's help page has the exact value).
2. If the domain never sends mail, use `v=spf1 -all`.
3. Run the scan again after DNS has updated.

dmarc_missing.title: No DMARC policy for {domain}
dmarc_missing.summary: {domain} handles e-mail but publishes no DMARC policy, so mail servers are not told what to do with e-mails that fail authentication.
dmarc_missing.why: DMARC ties SPF and DKIM together and tells receivers to quarantine or reject e-mails that fake your domain. Without it, most spoofed messages still get delivered, and you get no reports about who is sending mail in your name.
dmarc_missing.fix:
1. Start in monitoring mode: add a TXT record at `_dmarc.{domain}` with `v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc@{domain}`.
2. Check the reports for a couple of weeks and make sure all your real senders pass SPF or DKIM.
3. Then enforce: change to `p=quarantine` and later `p=reject`.
4. Run the scan again.

dmarc_not_enforced.title: DMARC for {domain} only monitors (p=none)
dmarc_not_enforced.summary: The DMARC policy that applies to {domain} is p=none: it reports, but it does not stop fake e-mails.
dmarc_not_enforced.why: p=none is the right first step, but spoofed e-mails in your name are still delivered normally. The protection only starts with p=quarantine or p=reject.
dmarc_not_enforced.fix:
1. Use the DMARC reports to confirm that all your real senders pass SPF or DKIM.
2. Change the policy to `p=quarantine` (optionally with `pct=` to ramp up), then to `p=reject`.
3. If the policy comes from your main domain's record, check its `sp=` value, which applies to subdomains.
4. Run the scan again.

open_resolver.title: Your nameserver answers DNS questions for anyone ({nameserver})
open_resolver.summary: {nameserver}, a nameserver of your domain, looks up names of other domains for any computer on the internet (an open resolver).
open_resolver.why: Open resolvers are abused to flood other networks (DNS amplification attacks) using your server and bandwidth, which can get your IP addresses blocklisted. They can also be used to poison cached answers. A nameserver for your domain only needs to answer questions about your own domain.
open_resolver.fix:
1. Turn off recursion for the public: in BIND set `recursion no;` (or `allow-recursion { localhost; your-networks; };`); in Unbound or PowerDNS Recursor, restrict `access-control` to your own networks.
2. If you use a managed DNS provider, this should never happen; contact their support.
3. Run the scan again.

zone_transfer_open.title: Anyone can download your whole DNS zone ({nameserver})
zone_transfer_open.summary: {nameserver} hands out a complete copy of your DNS zone (AXFR zone transfer) to anyone who asks.
zone_transfer_open.why: A zone transfer reveals every name in your domain: staging and internal servers, admin panels, mail and VPN hosts. That gives attackers a ready-made map of targets they would otherwise have to guess.
zone_transfer_open.fix:
1. Allow zone transfers only to your own secondary nameservers: in BIND `allow-transfer { secondary-ip; };`, in PowerDNS `allow-axfr-ips`, in Windows DNS "Zone Transfers" set to listed servers only.
2. Managed DNS providers usually block this by default; check the zone transfer setting in their dashboard.
3. Run the scan again.
